title: Components — symbols, thermistors and LDRs
examTip: Circuit symbols and sensor questions come up often. Know every symbol, and say what happens to resistance as light or temperature increases.
introTips: Learn every circuit symbol and draw them from memory
LDR: brighter light, less resistance. Thermistor: hotter, less resistance
You will draw a circuit to test a sensor
intro: Why do street lights switch on by themselves at dusk? How does a heating system know when a room is warm? Some components change their resistance with light or with heat. This lesson shows how they behave, and how to draw them.

basics.text: Current is how much electric charge flows past a point each second. Think of cars passing under a bridge: more cars each second is a bigger flow. It is measured in amperes (A), often called amps.
Potential difference is the push that makes charge move round a circuit. A cell or battery gives it. It is measured in volts (V), and a bigger number means a bigger push.

Resistance is how hard it is for current to get through something. It is like a narrow, crowded corridor that slows people down. More resistance means less current for the same push. It is measured in ohms (Ω).

basics.idea: The two axes of a graph
basics.text: A graph has a line across the bottom, called the x-axis. The line up the side is the y-axis. Each one shows a quantity you measured. Each point on the graph is one pair of readings.

The origin is the point on a graph where both quantities are zero. On many graphs it is the bottom-left corner. On some, the axes cross in the middle, and the origin is where they cross. A line "through the origin" means that when one quantity is zero, so is the other.
Two quantities are directly proportional when doubling one doubles the other. Apples are like this: twice as many apples cost twice as much. On a graph this is a straight line through the origin.
Light intensity means how bright the light is. A sunny window has a high light intensity. A dark cupboard has a low one.

keyPoints.heading: Circuit symbols — the language of circuit diagrams
keyPoints.content:
People draw circuits so that anyone can build them. Instead of drawing a real lamp or meter, they use simple shapes that everyone agrees on.

These shapes are <dfn>circuit symbols</dfn>, and a drawing made from them is a <dfn>circuit diagram</dfn>. Wires are drawn as straight lines. A <dfn>cell</dfn> is a long thin line next to a short thick one; two or more cells joined together make a <dfn>battery</dfn>. A resistor is a small rectangle. A lamp is a circle with a cross in it. A <dfn>switch</dfn> is drawn open, with a gap, or closed, with no gap. A meter is a circle with a letter: A for an ammeter, V for a voltmeter.

Some symbols are built from others. A resistor with an arrow through it is a variable resistor. A diode with two arrows coming out of it is a <dfn>light-emitting diode (LED)</dfn>, a diode that gives out light. A <dfn>fuse</dfn>, a safety part that cuts off a current that is too big, is a rectangle with a line through it.

To read a circuit diagram, follow the wire from one side of the cell round to the other. Components on one single path are in series. Components on separate branches are in parallel.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: The standard circuit symbols. Learn every one.
writeBullets: Every component has a standard symbol; wires are straight lines

keyPoints.heading: Thermistors — resistance that changes with temperature
keyPoints.content:
In an earlier lesson you saw that a filament lamp and a diode do not keep a fixed resistance. It changes as the current through them changes. The same is true of two components that react to the world around them: the <dfn>thermistor</dfn> and the <dfn>light-dependent resistor</dfn> (<dfn>LDR</dfn>).

First, the thermistor. Its resistance depends on its <dfn>temperature</dfn>, which is how hot it is. As a thermistor gets warmer, its resistance goes down. When it cools, its resistance goes back up. So for the same potential difference, a warm thermistor lets a bigger current through than a cold one.

That makes a thermistor a good temperature <dfn>sensor</dfn>: a part that detects a change around it. In a <dfn>thermostat</dfn>, the control that keeps a room or an oven at a set temperature, a thermistor senses how warm it is. When the room warms up, the thermistor's resistance falls, the current changes, and the circuit switches the heater off. When the room cools, the heater comes back on.

Its symbol is a resistor with a diagonal line through it that ends in a short flat tail.
writeBullets: Used as a temperature sensor, for example in a thermostat
Lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs: resistance changes with the current

definitions: As a thermistor gets hotter, its resistance decreases.
Lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs do not have a constant resistance; it changes with the current through them.
A thermistor is used to sense temperature, for example in a thermostat.

keyTerms.def: A component whose resistance decreases as its temperature increases.
A part that detects a change around it, such as a thermistor (temperature) or an LDR (light).
A control that keeps a room or an oven at a set temperature. It can use a thermistor to sense the temperature.

keyPoints.memTip: Thermistor: hot → low resistance. Cold → high resistance.

keyPoints.heading: LDRs — resistance that changes with light
keyPoints.content:
Some street lights come on by themselves as it gets dark. They use a light-dependent resistor, or LDR.

An LDR's resistance depends on how bright the light falling on it is: its <dfn>light intensity</dfn>. As the light gets brighter, its resistance goes down. In the dark, its resistance is high.

So an LDR is a light sensor. In an automatic light, the LDR's resistance rises as evening comes. The circuit detects that change and switches the light on. In the morning, the resistance falls again and the light switches off.

The LDR and the thermistor behave in the same way, so they are easy to mix up. Remember what each one senses: an LDR responds to light, a thermistor to temperature. For both, more of that thing means less resistance.

The symbol for an LDR is a resistor in a circle, with two arrows pointing in to show light falling on it.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: An LDR: brighter light, lower resistance.
writeBullets: LDR: brighter light means lower resistance
Used to switch lights on when it gets dark
An LDR senses light; a thermistor senses temperature

definitions: As light intensity increases, the resistance of an LDR decreases.
An LDR is used to sense light, for example to switch lights on when it gets dark.

keyTerms.def: A component whose resistance decreases as the light intensity on it increases.

keyPoints.memTip: LDR: Light Down Resistance. More light, less resistance.

keyPoints.heading: Drawing a circuit to test a sensor
keyPoints.content:
Exam questions often ask you to draw a circuit to find how a thermistor's or an LDR's resistance changes. You use the same idea as for any component: measure the current and the potential difference, then find the resistance.

Draw the cell, a switch and an ammeter in one loop with the thermistor, all in series. Then draw a voltmeter in parallel across the thermistor, on its own short branch. Use the correct symbol for every part, with straight lines for the wires and no gaps where wires should join.

Put the thermistor in water and measure the water's temperature with a thermometer. Record the current and the potential difference, then change the temperature and repeat. For an LDR, change the light intensity instead, for example by moving a lamp closer.

At each reading, divide the potential difference by the current to get the resistance. Plot resistance against temperature, or against light intensity: both graphs slope downwards.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: Testing a thermistor: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, thermistor in water.
writeBullets: Ammeter in series with the sensor; voltmeter in parallel across it
Change the temperature (or light) and record V and I each time

definitions: To find a resistance: ammeter in series with the component, voltmeter in parallel across it, then divide V by I.

workedExamples.question: A thermistor in cold water has a potential difference of 6 V across it and a current of 0.002 A through it. What is its resistance?

steps.text: You want R, so divide both sides by I: R = V ÷ I.

workedExamples.question: The water is heated. With the same 6 V, the current rises to 0.03 A. What is the resistance now?

steps.text: The resistance is 200 Ω: lower, because the thermistor is hotter.

keyPoints.memTip: Series A, Parallel V: the Ammeter goes in Series, the Voltmeter in Parallel.

0.question: Which component is drawn as a circle with a cross inside it?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. A lamp is a circle with a cross in it.
0.wrongFeedback: A lamp is a circle with a cross in it. Meters are circles with a letter: A for an ammeter, V for a voltmeter.

1.question: What happens to the resistance of a thermistor as it gets hotter?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. A hotter thermistor has a lower resistance.
1.wrongFeedback: As a thermistor gets hotter, its resistance decreases. It does not fall to zero.

2.question: An outdoor light switches on by itself when it gets dark. Which component senses the dark?
2.correctFeedback: Correct. An LDR senses light: its resistance rises as it gets dark.
2.wrongFeedback: An LDR senses light. As it gets dark, its resistance rises, and the circuit switches the light on. A thermistor senses temperature, not light.

3.question: You are testing how a thermistor's resistance changes. How should the voltmeter be connected?
3.correctFeedback: Correct. The voltmeter goes in parallel across the thermistor, to measure the potential difference across it.
3.wrongFeedback: The voltmeter must be in parallel across the thermistor, to measure the potential difference across it. The ammeter is the meter that goes in series.

commonMistakes: Drawing a resistor as a zigzag. The standard symbol is a small rectangle.
Thinking a diode has zero resistance in the reverse direction. It has very HIGH resistance. So only a very small current flows.
Mixing up the LDR and thermistor. An LDR responds to light. A thermistor responds to temperature. Both drop in resistance as their quantity increases.
Forgetting that an LED is a type of diode. So it only conducts in the forward direction. It will not light up if it is connected the wrong way round.
examTips: When describing an LDR or thermistor, always say what happens to resistance as light intensity or temperature increases.
For I-V graph questions, describe the shape exactly. For example: 'straight line through the origin', 'curve that gets less steep', or 'flat then sudden steep rise'. Vague answers lose marks.
For circuit questions, write down V = IR first and start from there. Most electricity questions link back to it.
revisionCardBullets: Fixed resistor: constant resistance at constant temperature. Its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin
Variable resistor (rheostat): resistance changed by hand. Used in dimmer switches
V = IR: potential difference = current × resistance
Diode: current in one direction only. Very high resistance in the reverse direction
LED: a diode that gives out light. Used in screens, traffic lights and energy-efficient bulbs
I-V graph for a diode: flat for negative V, steep rise in the forward direction
Resistance of lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant. It changes with the current
LDR uses: automatic street lights, burglar alarms, camera meters
Thermistor uses: thermostats, fire alarms, engine and medical temperature sensors
